title: TCF induction followed by radiotherapy
context_label: Head and neck cancer: induction chemotherapy
indication_text: Induction chemotherapy followed by radiotherapy for stage III or IV non-metastatic squamous cell cancer of the head and neck, following multidisciplinary assessment.
purpose: This chemotherapy is given before definitive treatment to shrink or control the head and neck cancer. The team explains how induction fits your overall treatment aim and why this particular schedule is appropriate.
schedule_label: Every 21 days for 4 planned induction cycles.
schedule_summary: Docetaxel 75 mg/m² and cisplatin 75 mg/m² are given on Day 1. Fluorouracil 750 mg/m² runs over 22 hours on each of Days 1–5. Induction repeats every 21 days for 4 planned cycles unless cancer progression or unacceptable side effects require a change.
administration_text: Day 1 includes docetaxel over 60 minutes and cisplatin over 2 hours, plus prescribed fluids, premedication and anti-sickness treatment. Fluorouracil 750 mg/m² runs over 22 hours on each of Days 1–5. Total attendance is longer than the drug infusion alone. Confirm inpatient or outpatient arrangements, any pump changes and final disconnection.
monitoring_summary: Before starting: full blood count, kidney and liver tests, and DPD assessment before first fluorouracil unless already tested. ECG is needed for compromised heart function; hearing assessment and measured kidney clearance are arranged when indicated. Discuss hearing, tinnitus, nerve symptoms, swallowing, weight, medicines and allergies. Full blood count and kidney and liver tests are required before each cycle. Report hearing, tinnitus, nerve, mouth, bowel and fluid-intake changes before dosing; additional tests depend on symptoms and results.

agents.name: Docetaxel
agents.explanation: Docetaxel stabilises tiny structures called microtubules. Cells need these to separate their chromosomes during division; disrupting the process can stop cancer cells multiplying. Healthy dividing cells are also affected.
agents.watch: Take prescribed steroid premedication. Report fever, lasting numbness, swelling, sore nails or infusion symptoms.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and sepsis
Hair loss, mouth soreness and fatigue

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Cisplatin links strands of DNA, the instructions inside cells, making it harder for cancer cells to repair damage and divide. Healthy cells may also be affected. Kidney function, hearing, blood counts and nerve symptoms help the team decide whether the next dose is safe.
agents.watch: Report reduced urine, persistent vomiting, tinnitus, hearing change or new tingling.
risks: Low blood counts and serious infection
Hearing loss or tinnitus, which can persist
Infusion reaction and effects on fertility

agents.name: Fluorouracil
agents.mechanism: Disrupts production of DNA and RNA
agents.explanation: Fluorouracil, often shortened to 5-FU, interferes with the building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, which cells need to grow. It runs through a vein over the prescribed hours. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) is an enzyme that breaks it down. Testing for DPD deficiency before treatment reduces risk but cannot rule out every severe reaction.
agents.watch: Report severe diarrhoea, mouth sores, chest pain, sudden confusion, sore palms or soles, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms.
risks: Low blood counts and serious infection
Rare severe neurological or early excessive toxicity

agents.name: Radiotherapy
agents.mechanism: Damages cancer cells in the planned treatment area
agents.explanation: Radiotherapy directs radiation at a carefully planned area. It is delivered on its own appointment calendar. Effects depend on which tissues receive radiation and can build up during the course or continue after it finishes.
agents.watch: Report difficulty swallowing, weight loss, mouth pain, skin breakdown or problems managing saliva.
risks: Dry mouth, taste and saliva changes
Skin reaction in the treated area
Some swallowing, saliva or tissue effects can be lasting

phases.label: Induction chemotherapy
phases.detail: Docetaxel 75 mg/m² and cisplatin 75 mg/m² are given on Day 1. Fluorouracil 750 mg/m² runs over 22 hours on each of Days 1–5. Induction repeats every 21 days for 4 planned cycles unless cancer progression or unacceptable side effects require a change.

phases.label: Later radiotherapy
phases.detail: If the cancer has not progressed and blood counts have recovered adequately, radiotherapy is planned 4–7 weeks after completion of chemotherapy. The radiation team confirms the actual dates and prescription. This is a later phase, not radiation given alongside all four TCF cycles. Surgery may be considered afterwards.

phases_note: If the cancer has not progressed and blood counts have recovered adequately, radiotherapy is planned 4–7 weeks after completion of chemotherapy. medicines_title: What each part of treatment does

timeline.label: Docetaxel
timeline.text: Docetaxel 75 mg/m² by IV infusion over 60 minutes on Day 1.

timeline.label: Cisplatin and fluids
timeline.text: Cisplatin 75 mg/m² over 2 hours, with prescribed hydration.

timeline.label: Fluorouracil infusions
timeline.text: Fluorouracil 750 mg/m² runs over 22 hours on each of Days 1–5.

timeline.label: Symptoms and recovery
timeline.text: Report symptoms at any time. Blood tests and clinical review determine the next dose.

day_groups.title: Day 1: three-drug treatment begins
day_groups.body: Docetaxel and cisplatin are given in the unit with prescribed premedication, fluids and anti-sickness medicines. Fluorouracil begins. Five 22-hour fluorouracil infusions on Days 1–5; confirm each change and the final disconnection time.
day_groups.action: Tell the team if steroid doses were missed, you feel unwell or you have new symptoms before treatment starts.

day_groups.title: Fluorouracil continues
day_groups.body: Fluorouracil 750 mg/m² runs over 22 hours on each of Days 1–5. Only trained staff connect, program, change or disconnect the infusion.
day_groups.action: Follow the line and pump instructions. Call for leakage, pain, swelling, damage or an infusion that appears to finish unexpectedly or stop.

day_groups.title: Recovery and review
day_groups.body: Follow the prescribed home medicine and growth-factor plan. Side effects may continue or appear between visits; no day is guaranteed free of risk.
day_groups.action: Keep blood-test and review appointments and call promptly if unwell.

urgent_extra: Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, sudden confusion, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms needs urgent assessment even if DPD testing was normal. Report reduced urine, hearing change, ringing in the ears or new numbness promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.
timeline_note: This 21-day picture describes induction only. Steroid premedication starts the day before docetaxel. Infusion finish times depend on the chosen prescription and actual start time; later radiation or chemoradiation has a separate calendar.
safety_note: Use your treating service’s written temperature threshold and urgent-contact plan. Fever, shivering or sudden illness can be serious even without a high temperature. Do not wait for the next visit. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure needs emergency help: call 112 or 999.
treatment_scope_notice: This guide covers NCCP 00324 induction and explains the next treatment stage. Doses and dates are confirmed by your team. Later treatment needs its own agreed prescription; do not carry induction medicines or support instructions into it automatically.
anatomy_note: The map shows where important effects may occur and which treatment may cause them. It is not a prediction that every effect will happen. Tell the team about new, severe or worsening symptoms; effects can continue after treatment finishes.
teachback: Can I explain which treatment phase I am in and how many induction cycles are planned? Do I know when to start steroid tablets and what to do if a dose is missed? Can I explain my exact fluorouracil infusion and disconnection plan? Do I know my growth-factor plan, urgent symptoms and verified out-of-hours contact route?
passport_visit_note: Record the actual date, treatment phase, medicines given, any delay or dose change, blood tests and next appointments. The treating service confirms all entries; this does not replace its clinical record.

Report symptoms promptly; extra blood or organ tests may be needed.
The team reviews recovery, results and earlier side effects before another dose or phase.

rows.label: Mouth, nutrition and swallowing

Review mouth pain, weight, drinking, swallowing and, during radiation, the treated skin.

Dietitian and speech and language plans adapt to symptoms and recovery.
Continue dental, nutrition and swallowing care as needed.

Discuss symptoms and the agreed treatment aim.
Examinations or scans may be arranged for a particular concern.
Response, recovery and your preferences inform the next treatment decision.

monitoring_schedule.note: Routine blood safety checks are different from tests ordered for a symptom and from scans used to assess the cancer. Your team supplies exact dates and explains results.

monitoring_test_details.label: Full blood count
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Checks white cells for infection protection, red cells for oxygen carriage and platelets for clotting.
monitoring_test_details.timing: At baseline and before every induction cycle.

monitoring_test_details.label: Kidney function and fluid balance
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Cisplatin can injure kidneys; results and hydration guide safe prescribing.
monitoring_test_details.timing: At baseline and before each cycle; extra checks or measured clearance when indicated.

monitoring_test_details.label: Liver function
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Helps assess whether the medicines, particularly docetaxel, can be given safely.
monitoring_test_details.timing: At baseline and before each cycle.

monitoring_test_details.label: DPD assessment before fluorouracil
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Reduced ability to break down fluorouracil can cause severe or life-threatening toxicity. Normal testing does not exclude every severe reaction.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Before first exposure unless already tested. Moderate or severe kidney impairment can make a blood-uracil phenotype harder to interpret; the team considers genotype testing where appropriate.

monitoring_test_details.label: Hearing assessment
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Checks hearing changes or ringing in the ears that cisplatin may cause.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Audiology when indicated; report hearing or tinnitus changes before each dose.

monitoring_test_details.label: Heart assessment / ECG
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Assesses existing heart problems and helps plan safe treatment; fluorouracil-related chest symptoms need urgent review.
monitoring_test_details.timing: ECG for compromised cardiac function; additional assessment for symptoms or clinician concern.

monitoring_test_details.label: Response assessment
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Helps decide the next treatment stage after induction.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Scans and examinations according to the individual treatment plan.

anatomy: Hair thinning or loss can occur. Ask about scalp care and practical support.
Ringing or hearing loss can persist (ototoxicity). Report a change before the next dose.
Soreness or ulcers (mucositis) can make eating and drinking difficult. Contact the team for pain or poor intake.
Chest pain can signal a heart effect (cardiotoxicity). Seek urgent assessment during or after the infusion.
Low white cells can cause serious infection; low platelets cause bruising or bleeding; anaemia causes fatigue. Call for fever or sudden illness.
Kidney injury and mineral changes can occur. Prescribed fluids and blood tests help protect you; report reduced urine or inability to drink.
Nausea and vomiting can occur; 5-FU may cause severe diarrhoea. Persistent symptoms can cause dehydration and need prompt help.
Docetaxel may affect nails and retain fluid; 5-FU may cause painful palms or soles (hand–foot syndrome). Report swelling, pain or skin breakdown.
Numbness or tingling (peripheral neuropathy) can persist. Report difficulty with buttons, walking or balance before another dose.
Dry mouth, taste change, sore skin and swallowing difficulty can build up. Some dental, saliva and swallowing effects last; follow the radiation care plan.

support.title: Steroid preparation for docetaxel
support.text: The source premedication is dexamethasone 8 mg by mouth twice daily for three days, starting the day before docetaxel, with at least three doses taken before infusion. It helps reduce allergy and fluid retention. Follow your prescribed plan. If doses are missed or you cannot swallow them, contact the unit before attending; the clinician decides the alternative.

support.title: One anti-sickness and steroid plan
support.text: Cisplatin has a high risk of nausea and vomiting. The team provides preventive and rescue anti-sickness treatment. Have all steroid doses reconciled on one list so the docetaxel premedication and anti-sickness prescription do not lead to accidental duplication.

support.title: Growth-factor support
support.text: Growth-factor support (G-CSF) may be prescribed according to your risks, blood counts and any earlier infection or low-count complication. It is not a universal all-cycle requirement in this source. If prescribed, confirm the product, injection dates and missed-dose instructions; fever or sudden illness still needs urgent contact.

support.title: Fluids and kidney protection
support.text: Cisplatin requires prescribed fluids before and after treatment. Oral hydration is encouraged for the following 24 hours, adapted to your heart, kidney and swallowing needs. Ask for a practical individual fluid plan and call for much less urine, persistent vomiting or inability to drink.

support.title: Antibiotics when prescribed
support.text: An antibiotic may be added by the treating team according to the regimen and your situation. It is not a medicine to start from an old supply. Confirm the name, start and stop dates and important interactions; infection symptoms still need urgent contact.

support.title: Food, mouth and swallowing support
support.text: Use the mouth-care and pain plan. Report ulcers, infection, poor intake or weight loss early. Dietitian and speech and language support can tailor intake and swallowing advice; arrange dental assessment before planned head and neck radiation.

support.title: Fertility, pregnancy and other medicines
support.text: Discuss fertility, pregnancy, breastfeeding and the medicine-specific duration of contraception before treatment. Bring medicines, supplements and allergies and check before adding over-the-counter or herbal products.

sections.title: Before the first visit
sections.text: Confirm the exact regimen, treatment aim, baseline tests, transport, support medicines and verified urgent contact numbers. Bring a full medicine list and any hearing, nerve or swallowing concerns.

sections.title: Time in the unit
sections.text: Day 1 includes docetaxel over 60 minutes and cisplatin over 2 hours, plus prescribed fluids, premedication and anti-sickness treatment. Fluorouracil 750 mg/m² runs over 22 hours on each of Days 1–5. Total attendance is longer than the drug infusion alone. Confirm inpatient or outpatient arrangements, any pump changes and final disconnection.

sections.title: Keeping appointments together
sections.text: Keep one calendar for blood tests, treatment and any radiation, dental, nutrition or swallowing appointments. If an appointment is cancelled, ask the relevant teams to agree the revised plan.

sections.title: Practical help
sections.text: Tell the team about travel, cost, work, caring responsibilities, communication or reading needs. Ask whether a support person or interpreter can attend and how treatment changes will be explained.

sections.title: Leaving the unit
sections.text: Check the next blood-test and treatment dates, medicine instructions and whom to call if unwell. Have the service confirm the daytime, out-of-hours and backup contact routes.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis
chapters.intro: Keep your diagnosis, treatment name and agreed goal with your records.

items.title: Site, type and stage
items.text: Ask where the cancer started, what the biopsy shows and how far it has spread. Site, stage, previous treatment and general health affect the available options.

items.title: Which pathway applies?
items.text: Induction chemotherapy followed by radiotherapy for stage III or IV non-metastatic squamous cell cancer of the head and neck, following multidisciplinary assessment.

items.title: Tumour tests and medicine safety tests
items.text: Your team explains any HPV/p16, Epstein–Barr virus or other tumour tests appropriate to your cancer site. Not every site needs the same tests. These are different from blood, kidney and other medicine safety checks.

chapters.title: Treatment choices and your priorities
chapters.intro: Discuss the whole plan and each stage before consenting.

items.title: Benefit and alternatives
items.text: This chemotherapy is given before definitive treatment to shrink or control the head and neck cancer. The team explains how induction fits your overall treatment aim and why this particular schedule is appropriate. Ask how the expected benefit and burdens compare with suitable alternatives and with your priorities.

items.title: When treatment changes
items.text: The clinician may delay, change or stop treatment because of symptoms, test results, response or your preferences. Record which component is affected and what must happen before restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription.

items.title: Understanding the next stage
items.text: If the cancer has not progressed and blood counts have recovered adequately, radiotherapy is planned 4–7 weeks after completion of chemotherapy. The radiation team confirms the actual dates and prescription. This is a later phase, not radiation given alongside all four TCF cycles. Surgery may be considered afterwards.

chapters.title: Preparing for and receiving treatment
chapters.intro: Plan the appointments and practical support around the exact prescription.

items.title: At the treatment visit
items.text: Day 1 includes docetaxel over 60 minutes and cisplatin over 2 hours, plus prescribed fluids, premedication and anti-sickness treatment. Fluorouracil 750 mg/m² runs over 22 hours on each of Days 1–5. Total attendance is longer than the drug infusion alone. Confirm inpatient or outpatient arrangements, any pump changes and final disconnection.

items.title: The treatment calendar
items.text: Docetaxel 75 mg/m² and cisplatin 75 mg/m² are given on Day 1. Fluorouracil 750 mg/m² runs over 22 hours on each of Days 1–5. Induction repeats every 21 days for 4 planned cycles unless cancer progression or unacceptable side effects require a change. This 21-day picture describes induction only. Steroid premedication starts the day before docetaxel. Infusion finish times depend on the chosen prescription and actual start time; later radiation or chemoradiation has a separate calendar.

items.title: Recording what was given
items.text: Write the actual date, phase, medicines and any change. Record a delayed or omitted dose clearly; it is not automatically made up. The wallet card gives a brief record and the passport keeps the fuller history.

chapters.title: Between visits: symptoms and medicines
chapters.intro: Use the written home plan and contact route.

items.title: Symptoms have no safe-day guarantee
items.text: Effects may begin during treatment or develop later, and some build up over repeated doses. Call for a new, severe or worsening symptom even when a calendar calls the day a recovery day.

items.title: One medicine list
items.text: Keep prevention medicines, rescue medicines and regular medicines together on one reconciled written list. Record what you take and whether it helps. Do not double a missed dose or reuse an old prescription unless your treating team instructs you.

items.title: When to seek help
items.text: Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, sudden confusion, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms needs urgent assessment even if DPD testing was normal. Report reduced urine, hearing change, ringing in the ears or new numbness promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.

chapters.title: Mouth, teeth and jaw care
chapters.intro: Dental preparation and gentle daily care reduce avoidable problems.

items.title: Before treatment
items.text: Arrange dental assessment before head and neck radiation. The dental and oncology teams decide what treatment is needed and how much healing time is required; do not schedule extractions independently.

items.title: During treatment
items.text: Follow the prescribed brushing, fluoride, rinse and pain-relief advice. Report ulcers, infection, new bleeding, difficulty wearing dentures or worsening jaw opening. Avoid starting a new mouthwash without checking if the mouth is sore.

items.title: After head and neck radiation
items.text: Dry mouth can increase dental problems and some radiation effects last. Keep regular dental care and tell any future dentist that you have had head and neck radiation before invasive treatment. Your radiation/dental team plans any procedure.

chapters.title: Eating, drinking and maintaining strength
chapters.intro: The aim is adequate intake and comfort during treatment.

items.title: Recognising an intake problem
items.text: Record weight and report food or drink becoming harder to manage. Pain, taste change, dry mouth or nausea can each need a different response; a dietitian can adapt the plan to you.

items.title: If ordinary food is not enough
items.text: The team may suggest food fortification, supplements or tube feeding when intake or swallowing safety requires it. A tube is a support option, not a judgement about how well you have tried to eat. Training and follow-up are needed.

items.title: Fluid needs are individual
items.text: Ask for a realistic drinking plan that accounts for kidney/heart problems and any feeding tube. Persistent vomiting, dizziness, markedly reduced urine or inability to drink needs urgent contact.

chapters.title: Swallowing, voice and communication
chapters.intro: A speech and language therapist can help protect function.

items.title: Swallowing assessment
items.text: Report coughing or choking with food or drink, a wet-sounding voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. The team may need to assess aspiration risk and safe textures.

items.title: Exercises and rehabilitation
items.text: Do swallowing or jaw exercises only as taught for your situation. Treatment and recovery can change what is comfortable and safe. Ask for reassessment when symptoms change.

items.title: Communication needs
items.text: Tell the team about changes in speech, voice or hearing. Ask for written instructions, communication aids, an interpreter or help involving a support person.

chapters.title: Daily life and emotional support
chapters.intro: Practical adjustments can make the plan easier to follow.

items.title: Energy and activity
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity according to your ability and team advice. Ask for help if weakness, falls, sleep difficulty or pain interferes with daily life.

items.title: Smoking and alcohol
items.text: Ask for support to stop smoking and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth irritation, medicine interactions and head and neck recovery can change what is safe for you.

items.title: Emotional and practical concerns
items.text: Tell the team about anxiety, appearance or intimacy concerns, finances, travel and caring responsibilities. Ask which local supports are available; resources can be added to your record when confirmed.

chapters.title: Recovery, assessment and longer-term care
chapters.intro: The last treatment and the end of recovery are different milestones.

items.title: Recovery and continuing effects
items.text: The team follows recovery and response before the next stage, including persistent kidney, hearing, nerve, mouth or bowel effects. Dental, nutrition and swallowing support may continue. Scans, examinations and any radiation-related late-effect tests follow your individual plan; no universal scan or blood tumour-marker schedule is set here.

items.title: Cancer assessment
items.text: Your team sets the examination and imaging plan for your cancer and symptoms. Record who arranges each test and who will explain the result. New or worsening symptoms should be reported rather than saved for the next routine scan.

items.title: Information for other clinicians
items.text: Keep the regimen name, treatment dates, ongoing medicines and relevant alert information. Tell future clinicians and dentists about head and neck radiation if you receive it, and about any persistent kidney, hearing, nerve or swallowing problem.

chapters.title: Your records and additional help
chapters.intro: Keep essential instructions available on paper.

items.title: The passport and wallet card
items.text: The three-page companion gives the essentials. Use the passport for the agreed plan, visits, test results, symptoms and questions. The wallet QR opens this exact treatment’s further information; it contains no personal clinical record.

items.title: Your urgent contact plan
items.text: Have the treating service enter and verify daytime, out-of-hours and backup numbers before relying on this pack. Keep the written contact and temperature instructions where you and a support person can find them.

items.title: If you prefer paper
items.text: Use the full printable handbook in its chapter order and write questions in the passport. You do not need to scan the QR or follow an internet link to use the essential treatment and safety information.

evidence.title: Understanding the evidence
evidence.intro: The NCCP regimen combines evidence and specialist guidance for a defined treatment setting.
evidence.population: Induction chemotherapy followed by radiotherapy for stage III or IV non-metastatic squamous cell cancer of the head and neck, following multidisciplinary assessment.
evidence.comparison: Your team compares this treatment with alternatives appropriate to your cancer site, stage, health and priorities.
evidence.interpretation: A treatment name such as TPF or chemoradiation does not make different dose schedules, patient groups or sequences interchangeable. Ask which research and clinical factors support your exact plan. No single study percentage is presented as your personal chance of benefit.
limitations: Research groups can differ in cancer site, stage, previous treatment and fitness.
The expected benefit and possible lasting effects must be discussed for your own situation.

consent_support: Discuss the individual aim, expected benefit, alternatives and uncertainty, including the role of induction before definitive treatment. Explain serious infection and sepsis, low blood counts and bleeding, nausea and dehydration, mouth and bowel toxicity, hair and nail changes, infusion allergy, fluid retention, lasting kidney/hearing/nerve damage, fluorouracil heart or early severe toxicity despite DPD testing, fertility and pregnancy, line/pump risks, steroid and growth-factor plans, and treatment burden. Later surgery, radiation or chemoradiation needs its own consent discussion.

questions.q: Why is chemotherapy given before the next treatment?
questions.a: This chemotherapy is given before definitive treatment to shrink or control the head and neck cancer. The team explains how induction fits your overall treatment aim and why this particular schedule is appropriate.

questions.q: Are all TPF or TCF schedules the same?
questions.a: No. This is NCCP 00324: docetaxel 75, cisplatin 75 and fluorouracil 750 mg/m², using the exact days and infusion times in this guide. There are 4 planned induction cycles. The name alone is not enough to identify the prescription.
Five 22-hour fluorouracil infusions on Days 1–5; confirm each change and the final disconnection time. Do not disconnect or change the infusion yourself.

questions.q: What if I miss the steroid tablets?
questions.a: Call the treatment unit before docetaxel. The clinician decides whether an alternative premedication or a change to the appointment is needed.

Growth-factor support (G-CSF) may be prescribed according to your risks, blood counts and any earlier infection or low-count complication. It is not a universal all-cycle requirement in this source. If prescribed, confirm the product, injection dates and missed-dose instructions; fever or sudden illness still needs urgent contact.

If the cancer has not progressed and blood counts have recovered adequately, radiotherapy is planned 4–7 weeks after completion of chemotherapy. The radiation team confirms the actual dates and prescription. This is a later phase, not radiation given alongside all four TCF cycles. Surgery may be considered afterwards.

questions.q: Does a normal DPD test mean fluorouracil cannot cause serious effects?
questions.a: No. Testing reduces risk but cannot exclude every severe reaction. Unexpectedly early severe diarrhoea, mouth pain, illness, chest pain or confusion still requires urgent assessment.

Blood count and kidney/liver tests; review hearing, nerves, mouth, bowels and hydration.
Response and recovery review; scans and further treatment follow your individual plan.

preparation: Bring your medicine list, appointment calendar and verified urgent contacts. Check steroid and growth-factor instructions.
